title: Big Ladle, Small Ladle
markdown:
The sun peeked. Gold light tickled Leo awake. Soup day. The cottage already smelled of onions and thyme. Fern the fawn twitched her nose in the doorway, then trotted to Aunt Rosa’s table as if the smell had sent her an invitation.

Leo was there, peeking at the soup pot. Steam fogged his fringe.

“Oh dear,” Aunt Rosa said, tipping the pot so they could see the bottom. “The pot is almost empty. We need more broth for friends.”

A line of bowls waited on the cloth. Friends would come with bread. The pot looked shy, as if it had already done its work and wanted a nap.

Leo pointed at the hook by the stove. “A big ladle!”

Fern nudged a smaller one, the one Rosa used for tasting. “This one is tiny.”

Aunt Rosa brought three bowls: tiny, medium, big. With the big ladle — swoosh — the big bowl was full in one go.

“Just enough for this one,” she said.

Leo took the small ladle. Plink, plonk. He poured into the tiny bowl. It filled just a little, a shiny puddle that did not reach the rim.

“This one holds much less,” he gasped.

He tried the small ladle in the big bowl next, just to see. Plink. Plonk. Plink. The big bowl still looked hungry. Fern watched, eyes sparkling. She took the medium ladle, the in-between one that sat in the crock.

“The big ladle fills the big bowl fast,” she murmured. “The small one fills the small bowl slow.”

“Exactly,” Aunt Rosa clapped, not calling them brilliant. “We need lots of soup, and we need it before the gate latch clicks. Let’s fill the big pot.”

Leo grinned. He grabbed the biggest ladle. Swoosh. Scoop and pour. Again and again. Broth climbed the pot’s sides, a rising tide. Fern helped with the biggest ladle too, her hooves careful on the stone floor. Faster and faster. A drop jumped and they laughed and wiped it with the cloth.

Soon the big pot bubbled, full of soup, the shy bottom gone. Rosa hung the small ladle back on its hook for tasting later, and left the big one in the pot because that was its job now.

“The bigger ladle holds more,” she said. “That made filling the pot so fast.”

Leo zipped from stove to table with the medium ladle, topping up the medium bowl until it matched the others. “We filled them up.”

Fern nodded. “The biggest ladle got the most soup with just a few quick scoops.”

Rosa set bread where the steam would warm it. “Different bowls hold different amounts. Different ladles do too.” She did not send them off to declare the day. She handed Leo the tasting ladle for one last check, and Fern carried napkins to the door.

Leo scooped a big spoonful into his own mouth, because testers must test. “Best soup day,” he declared, and meant the pot, the scoops, and the friends whose bowls were no longer empty.

Fern flicked an ear at the latch. Footsteps on the path. They set the full bowls in a row, big beside medium beside tiny, a little family of holds, and opened the door before the soup could think about getting cold.
